title: The unresolved production assumptions behind MSY-based fisheries management
content:
Abstract
Maximum sustainable yield (MSY) remains a central concept of fisheries science, management, and marine governance. Although contemporary stock assessments rarely rely on a simple logistic surplus-production model, MSY-oriented management continues to translate stock status and productivity expectations into allowable removals through reference points, proxies, harvest-control rules, quotas, and performance metrics. This Food for Thought article asks whether the production-to-harvest logic inherited from Schaefer’s synthesis still carries unresolved assumptions about bounded stock productivity, compensatory production, an interior maximum of sustainable removals, stationarity or slow variation in productivity, predictable recovery, and the accounting of natural mortality and other losses. Schaefer’s 1954 model is treated as the relevant historical starting point because it made MSY operational by joining logistic biomass growth, stock accounting, catch, and fishing effort in a form that could support harvest advice. Later fisheries science has substantially modified this framework through age-structured assessment, proxies for BMSY and FMSY, precautionary buffers, harvest-control rules, and management strategy evaluation. These developments have strengthened fisheries science, but they do not automatically remove the underlying conceptual problem; they relocate it to assumptions embedded in reference points, operating models, performance criteria, loss accounting, rebuilding expectations, and management implementation. Using western Baltic cod as an illustrative case, the article shows how MSY-oriented quota governance can become fragile when productivity, recruitment, age structure, natural mortality, ecosystem conditions, recovery capacity, and management implementation change together. The article does not argue for abandoning quantitative advice, legal reference points, or precautionary management. It argues for assumption-aware advice that distinguishes MSY as an institutional benchmark from MSY as a biological productivity claim and makes quota advice more explicitly conditional on tested or monitored recovery capacity, explicit treatment of losses, plausible implementation assumptions, and ecosystem conditions that determine whether a harvestable surplus still exists—that is, net production that can be removed without causing persistent stock decline or impairing recovery capacity. Re-examining the production assumptions behind MSY-based fisheries management can therefore strengthen harvest advice under changing ecological conditions.
